newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. reaches agreement with Zaire rebels on aid.
newsitem.headline: U.N. reaches agreement with Zaire rebels on aid.

text.p: The United Nations said on Wednesday it had reached agreement with rebel authorities in eastern Zaire to allow aid agencies to increase their presence and operations there.

Ben Parker of the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA) said the agreement was reached in the Zairean city of Goma on Tuesday between rebel leader Laurent Kabila and DHA Director Martin Griffiths.

"This presumably opens the door for a much accelerated presence of humanitarian organisations in Zaire but there still appear to be issues to be tackled through Kinshasa," Parker said. He could not say how quickly extra aid could now come.

The Zairean government has denounced aid being sent into a swathe of rebel-held territory in the east as a violation of its sovereignty. But U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali ordered it sent in on the grounds that it was urgently needed.

Zaire wants relief supplies for more than a million refugees and hundreds of thousands of Zaireans displaced by a rebellion to be sent through Kinshasa and airports such as Kisangani, hundreds of km (miles) from the heart of the revolt.
A small amount of medical supplies and food sent into Goma by U.N. and independent aid agencies on Monday has been held up at a football stadium while an agreement was negotiated with the rebels.

Tuesday's agreement established principles for humanitarian operations in eastern Zaire and said contacts with local authorities in the region could not be interpreted as foreign recognition of them or a violation of Zairean sovereignty.
It said all humanitarian workers would be given security guarantees and there would be an independent evaluation of needs and security and no restrictions placed on humanitarian personnel.

Aid workers said the rebels initially wanted to exclude French and Belgians and those aid workers who had previously worked in eastern Zaire. The rebels say aid agencies should be partly blamed for exiled Rwandan Hutu forces receiving arms.
All aid material will enter eastern Zaire through warehouses where it will be checked by local authorities to ensure there is no military material, such as arms or ammunition, included in it.
Liasion officers from the local authorities will be posted at frontier points and looted furniture, equipment and vehicles seized from aid agencies in eastern Zaire will be returned.
International agency vehicles are barred from carrying military personnel or material under the pact, Parker said.
